summary: The Heat of combustion calculator turns the heat of vaporization of water, number of moles of water vaporized and the heat of combustion into number of moles of fuel combusted. That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Heat of combustion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Heat of combustion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of moles of fuel combusted in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the fuel); then you type in the heat of vaporization of water, number of moles of water vaporized and the heat of combustion.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 11 options, such as custom, hydrogen and methane. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in megajoules per kilogram. The unit chip switches it to any of the 11 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in moles. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in megajoules per kilogram. The unit chip switches it to any of the 11 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Heat of combustion calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Number of moles of fuel combusted=-heat of vaporization of water × number of moles of water vaporized ÷ (lower heating value − heat of combustion)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in moles, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in megajoules per kilogram, and convertible to any of the 11 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Energy per mass, opening in megajoules per kilogram
  • Energy per mass, opening in megajoules per kilogram
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Energy per mass, opening in megajoules per kilogram

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Heat of combustion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the heat of vaporization of water, number of moles of water vaporized and the heat of combustion — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Heat of combustion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of moles of fuel combusted, derived from the heat of vaporization of water, number of moles of water vaporized and the heat of combustion. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Heat of combustion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the heat of vaporization of water, number of moles of water vaporized and the heat of combustion, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter lower heating value in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Lower heating value opens in megajoules per kilogram and the chip beside it offers 11 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Lower heating value = 0 MJ/kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Heat of combustion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
